steps.title: Key Point
steps.body: Punctuation is essential for AO6 (Technical Accuracy). Errors cost marks, but correct and sophisticated use can lift your writing to higher levels. Punctuation isn't just rules - it's about communication and effect.

steps.title: Effect
steps.body: Short sentences ending with full stops create a sense of finality, certainty, or drama. Each full stop is a pause, a breath, a moment of emphasis.

steps.title: Comma Splice Error
steps.body: Never join two complete sentences with just a comma. This is one of the most common punctuation errors in exams. Wrong: The door opened, she walked in. Right: The door opened. She walked in. Right: The door opened, and she walked in.

steps.title: Semi-Colon vs Full Stop
steps.body: A semi-colon suggests a closer connection than a full stop. Use it when you want to show that two sentences are thematically linked.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Add the missing punctuation: "the door opened she walked in slowly and looked around" | What's the difference between these two sentences? "The students' books" vs "The student's books" | When would you use a colon instead of a full stop?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: "The door opened. She walked in slowly and looked around." OR "The door opened. She walked in, slowly, and looked around." (Several acceptable versions depending on intended pace and emphasis.) | "The students' books" = the books belonging to multiple students (plural possession). "The student's books" = the books belonging to one student (singular possession). | Use a colon when the second part explains, illustrates, or expands on the first part. A full stop separates unrelated sentences. Colons create anticipation.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Leave 5 minutes at the end to proofread your work Read aloud in your head - hear where pauses should be Check every speech mark pair - open and close Double-check its/it's, your/you're, their/they're Use sophisticated punctuation (colons, semi-colons) for higher marks But only use punctuation you're confident with - errors cost marks Check apostrophes in every possessive noun Verify commas after fronted subordinate clauses
